title: Smooth Dynamic Cutoffs for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
claim: Fixed cutoffs give large, fluctuating neighbor counts; our dynamic cutoff holds a small constant count, sparsifying the graph.
layout: 2 stacked schematics left, 1 line plot right; contrast via color
description: The left column has two stacked schematics of an atom neighborhood. The top, labeled 'Dynamic Cutoff', shows blue atoms around a central atom, with two concentric dashed circles and green double arrows that show the radius expanding or shrinking. Only two atoms inside the circle connect to the center by arrows, and the outer atoms are left unconnected. The bottom, labeled 'Fixed Cutoff', uses orange atoms and one large dashed circle. Four atoms inside it all connect to the center by thicker arrows. On the right is a line plot of number of neighbors against time in picoseconds (0 to 100). The orange 'fixed' line fluctuates between about 52 and 85. The blue 'dynamic' line stays flat near 20. A legend sits below the plot. The eye goes first to the flat blue line against the noisy orange one.
caption: We introduce a dynamic cutoff function which induces graph sparsity onto the underlying atom graph while maintaining simulation stability. The dynamic cutoff function calculates a dynamic radius that targets a specific number of atoms to be within the dynamic radius while pruning the rest. This sparsification method leads to up to 2.26x reduction in memory consumption and up to 2.04x reduction in inference time depending on the model and atomic system.
abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have proven to be wildly useful for molecular dynamics simulations, powering countless drug and materials discovery applications. However, MLIPs face two primary bottlenecks preventing them from reaching realistic simulation scales: inference time and memory consumption. In this work, we address both issues by challenging the long-held belief that the cutoff radius for the MLIP must be held to a fixed, constant value. For the first time, we introduce a dynamic cutoff formulation that still leads to stable, long timescale molecular dynamics simulation. In introducing the dynamic cutoff, we are able to induce sparsity onto the underlying atom graph by targeting a specific number of neighbors per atom, significantly reducing both memory consumption and inference time. We show the effectiveness of a dynamic cutoff by implementing it onto 4 state of the art MLIPs: MACE, Nequip, Orbv3, and TensorNet, leading to 2.26x less memory consumption and 2.04x faster inference time, depending on the model and atomic system. We also perform an extensive error analysis and find that the dynamic cutoff models exhibit minimal accuracy dropoff compared to their fixed cutoff counterparts on both materials and molecular datasets. All model implementations and training code will be fully open sourced.
